problem: The symbol and unit are wrong. The temperature drop per atmosphere is dT/dp ≈ −0.0074 K per atmosphere, not dp/dT. dp/dT itself is the slope in Pa/K and is about −1.3 × 10⁷ Pa/K for ice-water, so a student who reads '−0.0074 K per atmosphere' as a value of dp/dT gets the quantity and its units confused.
fix: v_fus is negative, so dp/dT is negative, about −1.3 × 10⁷ Pa/K. Equivalently dT/dp ≈ −0.0074 K per atmosphere: the melting point of ice falls as pressure rises.

problem: 'Plot ln p against 1/T for a liquid and you get a straight line' is stated too strongly; the chapter has just said h_fg is only 'nearly constant for a short range'. Over a wide band the plot is a gentle curve.
fix: Plot ln p against 1/T over a modest range and the points fall close to a straight line; its slope gives an average h_fg for that range.

problem: The point 13.3 kPa at 323 K is the model's own prediction, not an input or a measured data point, and the plotted curve passes through it by construction. A student reading the figure sees perfect agreement, which contradicts the worked example saying the estimate is about 8 per cent above the steam-table value of about 12.3 kPa.
fix: Mark only the input 101.3 kPa at 373 K, and label 13.3 kPa as the model estimate (true value about 12.3 kPa), so the figure does not suggest exact agreement.

problem: 'The saturation curve meets the critical isotherm with a finite slope' is unclear. On a p-T diagram the critical isotherm is the vertical line T = T_c and is not something the curve meets with a slope; the intended point is simply that the slope stays finite at the critical point.
fix: The ratio h_fg/(T v_fg) keeps a finite limit as both tend to zero, so the vapour-pressure curve ends at the critical point with a finite slope; it does not become infinite. Finding the value needs the limiting ratio, not the separate values.

where: Lead and Section 3, skate blade example
problem: Pressure melting is now considered only a minor part of why a skate glides; friction and the natural liquid-like surface layer of ice do most of the work, and pressure alone lowers the melting point by well under a kelvin. The claim in the lead is a simplification presented as fact.
fix: Use the weighted wire through ice (regelation) as the example: the wire's pressure melts ice below it and the water refreezes above, so the block ends whole. If skating is mentioned, say pressure melting is only one contributor, along with friction.
